The information should be sent to the CAC in a password protected format with the password sent in a separate email.

4.7 Once it has provided this information the employer must inform the CAC, as soon as reasonably practicable, of any worker who leaves the bargaining unit. Please note: this duty only relates to leavers and not to those that may join the bargaining unit after application day. If the employer fails to supply the required information or fails to supply it in accordance with the statutory criteria and the application is in progress, the employer may be ordered to remedy the failure as the CAC considers reasonable. If the employer fails to comply with a remedial order the CAC may issue a declaration that the union is recognised as entitled to conduct collective bargaining on behalf of the workers constituting the bargaining unit.

4.8 The information provided by the employer will not be copied to the union although it will be informed of the number of workers on the list and the categories of workers. The list will be used for any checks required during the course of the application and for a ballot, should one be held. The information will be destroyed once the application has reached a conclusion.

Admissibility tests

4.9 The Schedule requires that, before the CAC can formally accept an application, it must first consider whether a valid formal request was made to the employer and whether the timescales described under Stage 1 and 2 above have been observed. Before accepting an application, the CAC must also apply a number of admissibility tests and it must consider evidence given to it by the employer and the union when it considers the tests. The tests are described below.

Is the application in the proper form (paragraph 33 of Schedule A1)? The CAC application form can be found on the CAC website. The application form must be accompanied by a copy of the formal request and any response received from the employer otherwise it will be rejected.

Has the application been received by employer (paragraph 34)? The CAC cannot accept any application unless the union has copied it to the employer, together with any supporting documents. Unions should consider sending documentation in a way in which it can be shown that they have been delivered.

Does the union have a certificate of independence from the Certification Office (paragraph 6)? The CAC cannot accept applications from trade unions that do not hold a current Certificate of Independence.

Does the employer employ at least 21 workers (paragraph 7)? If the employer, together with any associated employer(s), employs fewer than 21 workers, the statutory recognition procedure does not apply. This limitation applies to all workers employed, not just those in the bargaining unit. In determining the numbers of workers, part-time workers count as whole numbers. Temporary workers are counted if they are directly employed by the employer; those employed by agencies generally do not count. Please note: under the Agency Workers Regulations 2010 an agency worker whose contract with a temporary work agency is not a contract of employment is to be treated as having a contract of employment with the temporary work agency during an assignment with an employer. If employers and trade unions are unsure as to the status of any workers and, in particular, whether or not individuals meet the definition of “worker” in the 1992 Act, they may wish to take their own legal advice

Is there a competing application (paragraphs 14 and 38)? The CAC cannot adjudicate between competing applications which relate to the same or overlapping bargaining units. If only one of the unions making an application has at least the required membership (currently 10%) in the bargaining unit, the CAC will only consider that application and is required to reject all others. If more than one application has the required membership, the CAC cannot accept any of them and must reject them all. Please note that, in this context, bargaining units which have just one worker in common count as overlapping.

Is there an existing recognition agreement (paragraph 35)? The CAC cannot accept an application if there is an existing agreement under which a union is entitled to conduct collective bargaining on behalf of any workers in the bargaining unit. For this purpose, the existing agreement can be with any trade union, whether or not it has a certificate of independence, and can be a voluntary or statutory agreement. Equally, an existing collective agreement does not need to cover hours, pay or holidays (subject to (b) below) as long as it covers one or more of the matters specified in section 178 of the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992. The existing agreement only needs to cover one worker in the bargaining unit to make the application inadmissible although this does not apply if the worker or workers joined the bargaining unit after application day. There are three exceptions to the rule about existing agreements.

a) if the union recognised is a non-independent union that was de-recognised in the preceding three years, then an application from an independent union can be accepted. Without this provision an employer attempting to avoid statutory recognition could simply re-recognise a non-independent union (or staff association) as soon as it was de-recognised following an application (under part VI of the Schedule) from a worker, therefore barring the independent union indefinitely.

b) if there is an existing agreement with the same union that is making the application, and the existing agreement does not cover all of the following: pay, hours and holidays, then the application can still be accepted.

The CAC must pass all information it receives to the SIP as soon as possible. The CAC will not pass on the information to anyone else.

4.26 In the event that the employer does not comply with these duties the CAC may, if the initial period has not yet ended, order the employer to remedy the failure within a set timescale. Given the seriousness of the available penalty (see paragraph 4.27 below), the Panel will spell out the consequences of not complying with an order from the CAC when it is made. If the employer fails to comply with the order the CAC, again providing the initial period has not yet ended, will issue a notice to both parties confirming that there has been a failure to comply with the remedial order; this notice will spell out the consequences of the failure to comply with the remedial order.

Penalties for non-compliance with a CAC remedial order

4.27 If the CAC issues a notice confirming that the employer has failed to comply with the remedial order then it may also issue a declaration that the union is recognised. This will only occur where the CAC is also satisfied that;

the bargaining unit has been agreed by the parties or has been decided by the CAC; and

the agreed or decided bargaining unit has not led to the application being invalid (see 6.4 below); and

the initial period has not yet ended.

If the CAC is not satisfied that these conditions are met then no declaration will be issued until such time as they are met.

Union access to workers after acceptance of application

4.28 The union may also, by giving notice to the CAC and the employer, request access to the relevant workers in connection with the application to allow the union to inform the workers of the object of the application or any ballot arising from it and seek their support and their opinions on the issues involved. Any request for access is valid only if it is made before the end of the period of 5 working days starting with the day after the day on which the CAC gives notice that the application is accepted. There is no provision that allows the CAC to extend this period nor are there any further opportunities for a union to request physical access later in the process for example, at the time the CAC orders that a ballot be held although a union may still communicate with workers in the bargaining unit during the balloting period via the QIP– see paragraph 8.8 below.

4.29 If the union requests access within the 5 working day period the CAC must try to help the parties to reach agreement as to terms on which the union is to have access to the relevant workers within 20 working days starting with the day after the day on which the CAC gave notice that the application is accepted. If no agreement can be reached by the end of that period, the CAC will decide the terms of access (see paragraph 5.6 below). However, if during the 20 working day period, the CAC concludes that there is no reasonable prospect of the parties’ agreeing terms on which the union is to have access to the relevant workers, the CAC may give notice to the parties that the negotiation period ends with the date of the notice. The CAC must provide reasons for reaching this conclusion. The parties may also apply to the CAC for a declaration that the negotiation period is to end earlier or later than it would otherwise and the CAC may, by a notice given to the parties, declare that the negotiation period ends with the specified date by the parties. If the parties reach agreement as to access without CAC intervention a copy of the agreement should be sent to the CAC case manager. If no agreement is reached in the appropriate period, then the CAC must determine the access arrangements, if any. The CAC has 10 working days in which to do so, although this can be extended as long as the CAC gives notice to this effect with reasons. There is more information about this stage of the procedure in the Code of Practice on Access and Unfair Practices During the Recognition and Derecognition Process.

4.30 The parties must comply with the access arrangements whether they are agreed or determined by the CAC. The employer must also refrain from making any offer to any or all of the relevant workers which has or is likely to have the effect of inducing any or all of them not to attend any relevant meeting between the union and the relevant workers and is not reasonable in the circumstances.

4.31 The employer must also refrain from taking, or threatening to take, any action against a worker solely or mainly on the grounds that the worker attended or took part in any relevant meeting between the union and the relevant workers or indicated an intention to attend or take part in such a meeting. Paragraph 5.9-5.11 sets out the penalties for a failure to comply with an access arrangement as well as an employer’s failure to comply with its duties in this paragraph and 4.30 above).

Duty on the parties to refrain from using an unfair practice

4.32 Once the CAC has given notice that the application has been accepted, both the union and the employer must refrain from using any ‘unfair practice’ in relation to the application. The Code of Practice on Access and Unfair Practices During the Recognition and Derecognition Process provides guidance on the unfair practices.

4.33 Either the union and employer can complain to the CAC if they believe the other has used an unfair practice and the CAC must decide whether the complaint is ‘well founded’. A complaint will be well founded if the CAC finds that a party used an unfair practice. The CAC no longer has to be satisfied that the unfair practice changed or was likely to change a relevant worker’s intention to vote or abstain from voting, intention to vote a particular way or how they actually did vote.

2.4 There are also statutory procedures for de-recognition, the impact on statutory recognition of changes to the bargaining unit and specifying a method of bargaining where the parties have reached a semi-voluntary agreement. These are briefly summarised in Annex 2 and separate Guides for those procedures are available by email from the CAC and on the CAC’s website.

CAC Proceedings

3.1 The CAC will be even-handed in its application of the legislation. The procedures will be as user-friendly for both employers and trade unions as possible. Applications for statutory recognition may be made to the CAC if a direct request to the employer does not result in recognition.

3.2 On receipt, an application will be checked to ensure that all of the relevant questions have been answered and that it is made in line with the statute before being allocated to a CAC case manager, a member of the Secretariat. Incomplete applications will be returned to unions for resubmission and applications not accompanied by documents that are specified by the CAC will be rejected. The existence of each registered application will be made public on the CAC website.

3.3 A Panel of three CAC members will be appointed to deal with each application. The Panel will consist of the CAC Chair or, more usually, one of the Deputies and one Member with experience as a representative of employers and one Member with experience as a representative of workers. While the composition of the Panel will normally remain the same throughout an application, it may be necessary to change the membership in the event of unavailability of one of the members. Both parties will be informed of the names of the Panel members, and of any changes in the composition of the Panel.

3.4 The case manager will be the main point of parties’ contact, making enquiries of the parties on the instructions of the Panel. They will ensure that correspondence and documents are cross copied between the parties and the Panel as appropriate. The case manager will explain the statutory procedures and help both parties understand the implications of the legislation, as well as resolve difficulties. Either party can contact the case manager with queries concerning the application and the statutory procedure; the case manager can quickly liaise with the Panel where necessary. Should the case manager be out of the office for any reason, another CAC official will handle the case in their absence.

3.5 The CAC’s approach will be as flexible as possible, given that the processes are laid down in legislation and are quite formal in nature. The CAC will try to take a problem-solving approach and to help the parties, reach voluntary agreements outside the statutory process. Both parties are free to contact the case manager at any time to discuss the application. The CAC will make decisions based on the submissions and evidence put before it by the parties. It will be for the parties to take the initiative in developing their submissions and marshalling their evidence in preparation for each decision point. The onus is on a party that wishes to have an issue considered to raise it formally with the CAC.

3.6 Since the CAC has a duty to help the parties to resolve underlying problems and reach agreement, some contacts between the CAC and the parties will be of an informal nature. However, the CAC also has to take formal decisions based on evidence available to both parties, so there is a mix of informal and formal processes. Where necessary, the case manager and Panel members will make it clear to the parties when they are discussing matters informally and when the discussion is part of a formal process.

3.7 Whilst not all decision points will arise in every case, the key CAC decision points are:

whether to accept the application (in all cases);

what, if any, are the terms on which the union is to have access to the relevant workers

what the bargaining unit should be;

if the bargaining unit agreed or decided is different from that in the original application, whether the application is valid;

whether a ballot is needed, and how it is to be conducted;

what the method of conducting collective bargaining should be.

Time

3.8 Time periods in the Schedule are measured in ‘working days’. The Schedule defines a working day as a day other than a Saturday or a Sunday, Christmas day or Good Friday, or a day which is a bank holiday under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971 in the relevant part of Great Britain.
